subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 2-year-old boy of West African ancestry is brought to the emergency department with severe pain and swelling of the hands and feet, pallor, and scleral icterus. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL and the reticulocyte count is 11%; the peripheral smear shows sickle-shaped red cells. Sequencing of the beta-globin gene reveals a single base change in the sixth codon, from GAG to GTG.
question: Which of the following best classifies this mutation?

options.text: Silent mutation, because the substitution occurs within a codon but does not change the amino acid sequence.
Nonsense mutation, because the new codon is read as a termination signal.
Frameshift insertion, because an extra nucleotide is added to the coding sequence.
Transversion causing a missense mutation, because a purine is replaced by a pyrimidine and the amino acid changes.
Transition causing a missense mutation, because one purine is replaced by another purine.

explanation_correct: In GAG to GTG, adenine (a purine) is replaced by thymine (a pyrimidine), which is a transversion. The codon changes from glutamate to valine, so one amino acid is substituted for another (missense), producing hemoglobin S. The new hydrophobic surface patch drives polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin S and the sickling seen on the smear.

explanation_incorrect.A: A silent mutation encodes the same amino acid; here glutamate is replaced by valine, so the protein sequence does change.
explanation_incorrect.B: GTG is not a stop codon; the three stop codons are UAA, UAG, and UGA.
explanation_incorrect.C: No nucleotide is inserted; this is a single nucleotide substitution, not an insertion, so the reading frame is preserved.
explanation_incorrect.E: A transition is a purine-to-purine or pyrimidine-to-pyrimidine change (for example, A to G); adenine to thymine is a transversion.

educationalObjective: The Glu6Val substitution of sickle cell disease is a purine-to-pyrimidine transversion that causes a missense change and creates a hydrophobic surface patch on hemoglobin S.
